## agent-ml-research
ML research experiment management tools

attachment.content:
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

  - section: method
    word_budget: 1000
    core_bullets:
      - "Problem formulation: given LLM M, input x, N stochastic samples {y_1,...,y_N}, define confidence signal c(x, {y_i}) → ℝ"
      - "Signal 1 — Log-probability: c_lp(y_i) = (1/|y_i|) Σ log p(t_j|t_{<j}, x). Per-sample signal. Clarify: sequence-level mean, not token-level max."
      - "Signal 2 — Exact-match voting: c_em(x) = max_y |{i: y_i = y}| / N. Instance-level."
      - "Signal 3 — Fleiss' Kappa (FK): token-level inter-rater agreement. Instance-level."
      - "Signal 4 — Soft Jaccard (SJ): set-aware structural similarity via type-grouped bipartite matching. Instance-level. Key: uses Hungarian matching with max(|A|,|B|) normalization."
      - "Signal 5 — Entity voting confidence: per-entity majority voting rate, averaged. Instance-level."
      - "Distinction: log-prob is PER-SAMPLE (ranks candidates), others are INSTANCE-LEVEL (aggregate across samples). This distinction is central to the correlation-selection gap."
      - "Evaluation: quality estimation (ρ, τ, AUROC vs F1) and sample selection (best-of-N F1)"

    type: statistical
    tool: matplotlib
    description: >

      Shows which signals are well-calibrated vs overconfident. Focus on SJ, voting_conf, logprob (3 curves per panel).
    caption_notes: >
      Caption or surrounding text MUST note two definition differences:
      (1) F1 definition: y-axis uses mean_sample_f1 (average F1 across N stochastic samples per instance),
      distinct from greedy F1 used in Table 1 ρ/AUROC targets — this is the calibration-appropriate measure
      since confidence signals aggregate over stochastic samples.

      naturally [0,1]). ECE absolute values are therefore NOT directly comparable across signals — only
      relative calibration patterns (over/under-confident regions) are meaningful.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Implications for practitioners.}
All signals achieve positive quality estimation across non-collapsed datasets (LP $\rho{=}0.42$ on Few-NERD, VC $\rho{=}0.38$ on SciERC, EM AUROC${=}0.82$ on CoNLL), with rankings stable across model families and a 4B ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}).
For selection, LP achieves significant gains only when both conditions are met ($+1.36$~pp on Few-NERD, $p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}); structural signals uniformly degrade selection.
RE signal rankings are in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.

\paragraph{Why the gap exists.}
Two mechanisms block selection: \textit{instance degeneracy} (consensus-proximity) and \textit{weak LP-quality alignment} (per-sample).
Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} correlates positively with F1 (SJ median $\rho{=}0.524$) and closes 23--41\% of the oracle gap, but 17.8\% (SciERC) to 47.4\% (CoNLL) of instances produce identical F1 across all samples, eliminating headroom entirely (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
Degeneracy is determined by the interplay of task structure, model architecture, and training convergence (Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}); cross-model evidence (LLaMA 89.2\% vs.\ Qwen 47.4\% on CoNLL; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}) reinforces the pattern.
LP is severely compressed (median range 0.041 nats; Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}), with pooled within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}){=}0.248$.

\paragraph{Non-tied subset and $N$-scaling.}
Where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), within-instance $\rho$ rises to 0.39 and LP selection yields $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$, survives Bonferroni; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}).
LP scales with $N$ in the low-degeneracy regime ($+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16 on Few-NERD, $p{=}0.003$; \S\ref{sec:fewnerd}); on SciERC, even $N{=}32$ captures less than 5\% of headroom (Table~\ref{tab:n_scaling_selection}).
An oracle tiebreaker within VC-equivalent groups recovers $+7.9$~pp, confirming per-sample signal exists but current signals cannot extract it (full analyses in Appendices~\ref{app:n_scaling}, \ref{app:verbalized_confidence}, \ref{app:vc_quartile}).

\paragraph{LP compression mechanisms.}
Four non-mutually-exclusive mechanisms contribute: token-level averaging, schema-dominated tokens, vocabulary restriction under constrained decoding, and format-token dilution.
Free-form decoding rules out constraint-imposed mechanisms for NER (std ratio 0.97; Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}) but restores LP selection for RE ($+2.35$~pp, $p{=}0.025$; Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
Entity-token LP exhibits $4{\times}$ higher variance yet performs worse ($-2.0$~pp SciERC, $-3.3$~pp CoNLL): fine-tuned models assign near-deterministic probabilities at the representation level, and compression cannot be broken by disaggregating to entity tokens.
LP failures show cross-seed stability (Jaccard${=}0.42$; Appendix~\ref{app:lp_failure_stability}), consistent with a systematic failure mode.

\paragraph{Regime boundaries.}
At the low-resource boundary (WNUT-17), QE signals collapse (VC conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}); at the ceiling boundary (CoNLL, degeneracy 47--89\%), LP does not improve selection.
In the moderate regime, two conditions jointly determine effectiveness: the cross-dataset gradient (47\% $\to$ n.s., 18\% $\to$ $+0.42$~pp, 14\% $\to$ $+1.36$~pp) is consistent with an inverse relationship ($n{=}3$ datasets), with stronger grounding from per-entity-type analysis ($\rho{=}{-}0.881$, $p{=}0.004$, $n{=}8$; Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
Temperature manipulation provides the cleanest test ($T{=}1.2$: degeneracy 12.5\%, $\rho{=}0.225$; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}), altering output diversity without changing model capacity.
LoRA rank${=}8$ (degeneracy 7.2\%, $\rho{=}0.24$) corroborates the pattern, though this ablation conflates diversity with capacity; both confirm that alignment is largely task-determined, and degeneracy reduction alone cannot unlock LP selection on datasets with weak alignment.

\paragraph{Practical guidelines.}
Practitioners should first estimate instance degeneracy on a labeled subset (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}): in the high-degeneracy regime (${>}$30\%), prefer greedy decoding; structural signals still support quality estimation ($\rho{=}0.43$--$0.47$).
In the low-degeneracy regime (${<}$15\%) with adequate alignment ($\rho \gtrsim 0.3$), LP selection is effective and scales with $N$ ($+1.36$~pp on Few-NERD; $+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16).
Temperature provides a controllable lever for degeneracy (40.3\% at $T{=}0.5$ to 12.5\% at $T{=}1.2$; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}) but cannot address alignment; training convergence offers a second lever (Few-NERD degeneracy rises from 11\% to 31\% between 3 and 5 epochs, halving LP gains; on SciERC, 3-epoch training yields 6.4\% degeneracy with FK $\rho{=}0.53$, SJ $\rho{=}0.52$, vs.\ 17.8\% and FK $0.27$, SJ $0.36$ at 5 epochs; Table~\ref{tab:epoch_confound}).
Standard calibration methods preserve within-instance argmax and cannot change selection; even multi-feature variants yield no improvement ($p{=}0.31$--$0.83$; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration_baseline}), confirming the bottleneck is alignment rather than miscalibration.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal; even supervised combination of the five signals studied does not close the oracle gap (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}).
Effective selection requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}; $N{=}8$ captures most QE benefit (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
Structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).

\section{Few-NERD Epoch Confound Analysis}\label{app:epoch_confound}

\paragraph{Training convergence modulates degeneracy.}
Table~\ref{tab:epoch_confound} compares the 3-epoch model (used throughout the main text) with a 5-epoch variant on Few-NERD (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$).
Extended training increases greedy F1 by $+2.95$~pp (0.748 $\to$ 0.777) but nearly triples instance degeneracy (11.1\% $\to$ 31.3\%), reducing the fraction of instances with non-degenerate outputs from 85.6\% to 68.7\%.
LP selection gains drop correspondingly ($+1.37$~pp $\to$ $+0.62$~pp), consistent with the degeneracy-gating mechanism identified in the main text (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Within-instance LP-quality alignment is relatively stable under this convergence shift (mean $\rho$: $0.524 \to 0.407$; median $\rho$: $0.667 \to 0.615$), consistent with alignment being determined primarily by task structure rather than training duration.

Evaluation loss increases after epoch 3 (0.032 $\to$ 0.041 at epoch 5), and the best checkpoint by validation loss occurs at step 32{,}000 (approximately epoch 3.9).
Standard early stopping practice thus naturally selects the low-degeneracy regime where LP selection is most effective.
This finding refines the narrative: degeneracy is not a fixed property of datasets but is modulated by the degree of training convergence. Over-trained models compress their output distributions, collapsing diversity even on datasets that support it under well-regularized training.

1	Our evaluation covers four NER datasets; an exploratory RE extension on SciERC is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension} but generalization to other RE benchmarks remains unvalidated.
2	We cover 4B\textendash 8B scale; whether the gap holds for 70B+ models or closed-source APIs is untested. Larger models may produce more diverse samples.
3	We do not train a verifier, leaving unknown how much oracle headroom a supervised approach could recover.
4	
5	We evaluate at $N{=}8$ (primary) and $N{=}16$; behavior at larger sample sizes is unknown (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
6	The free-form ablation covers SciERC NER and CoNLL NER with one model; RE free-form results are in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
7	Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint used empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks; a three-part analysis rules out this confound (Appendix~\ref{app:thinking_token}).
8	LP compression worsens on easy datasets at lower temperature (CoNLL tied fractions reach 95.8\% at $T{=}0.7$); whether reduced temperature translates to selection gains remains untested.
9	We tested verbalized confidence \cite{tian2023calibration} as a second per-sample signal; it exhibits severe overconfidence (mean 8.58/10 on SciERC, 9.24/10 on CoNLL) and yields the weakest QE and selection among all signals (Appendix~\ref{app:verbalized_confidence}).

\paragraph{SciERC epoch curve.}
Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc} extends the analysis to SciERC with a 3-point curve (3, 5, 10 epochs; Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$).
Degeneracy increases monotonically (6.4\% $\to$ 17.8\% $\to$ 47.8\%), but critically, within-instance LP-quality correlation also degrades: median $\rho$ drops from 0.317 at 3 epochs to 0.120 at 10 epochs, indicating that overtraining erodes both necessary conditions simultaneously.
At 10 epochs, the model retains competitive greedy F1 (0.649 vs.\ 0.650 at 3 epochs) with 8.4~pp of oracle headroom, yet LP selection yields only $+0.75$~pp, consistent with weak within-instance alignment ($\rho{=}0.120$) rather than effective signal exploitation.
This pattern validates the two-condition framework (\S\ref{sec:discussion}): at 10 epochs, condition~1 is violated (47.8\% degenerate) and condition~2 is compromised ($\rho{=}0.120$).
The gradient confirms that consistency-based signals are most effective at moderate training convergence; extended training compresses output distributions, degrading both diversity and within-instance alignment.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Implications for practitioners.}
All signals achieve positive quality estimation across non-collapsed datasets (LP $\rho{=}0.42$ on Few-NERD, VC $\rho{=}0.38$ on SciERC, EM AUROC${=}0.82$ on CoNLL), with rankings stable across model families and a 4B ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}).
For selection, LP achieves significant gains only when both conditions are met ($+1.36$~pp on Few-NERD, $p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}); structural signals uniformly degrade selection.
RE signal rankings are in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.

\paragraph{Why the gap exists.}
Two mechanisms block selection: \textit{instance degeneracy} (consensus-proximity) and \textit{weak LP-quality alignment} (per-sample).
Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} correlates positively with F1 (SJ median $\rho{=}0.524$) and closes 23--41\% of the oracle gap, but 17.8\% (SciERC) to 47.4\% (CoNLL) of instances produce identical F1 across all samples, eliminating headroom entirely (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
Degeneracy is determined by the interplay of task structure, model architecture, and training convergence (Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}); cross-model evidence (LLaMA 89.2\% vs.\ Qwen 47.4\% on CoNLL; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}) reinforces the pattern.
LP is severely compressed (median range 0.041 nats; Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}), with pooled within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}){=}0.248$.

\paragraph{Non-tied subset and $N$-scaling.}
Where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), within-instance $\rho$ rises to 0.39 and LP selection yields $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$, survives Bonferroni; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}).
LP scales with $N$ in the low-degeneracy regime ($+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16 on Few-NERD, $p{=}0.003$; \S\ref{sec:fewnerd}); on SciERC, even $N{=}32$ captures less than 5\% of headroom (Table~\ref{tab:n_scaling_selection}).
An oracle tiebreaker within VC-equivalent groups recovers $+7.9$~pp, confirming per-sample signal exists but current signals cannot extract it (full analyses in Appendices~\ref{app:n_scaling}, \ref{app:verbalized_confidence}, \ref{app:vc_quartile}).

\paragraph{LP compression mechanisms.}
Four non-mutually-exclusive mechanisms contribute: token-level averaging, schema-dominated tokens, vocabulary restriction under constrained decoding, and format-token dilution.
Free-form decoding rules out constraint-imposed mechanisms for NER (std ratio 0.97; Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}) but restores LP selection for RE ($+2.35$~pp, $p{=}0.025$; Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
Entity-token LP exhibits $4{\times}$ higher variance yet performs worse ($-2.0$~pp SciERC, $-3.3$~pp CoNLL): fine-tuned models assign near-deterministic probabilities at the representation level, and compression cannot be broken by disaggregating to entity tokens.
LP failures show cross-seed stability (Jaccard${=}0.42$; Appendix~\ref{app:lp_failure_stability}), consistent with a systematic failure mode.

\paragraph{Regime boundaries.}
At the low-resource boundary (WNUT-17), QE signals collapse (VC conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}); at the ceiling boundary (CoNLL, degeneracy 47--89\%), LP does not improve selection.
In the moderate regime, two conditions jointly determine effectiveness: the cross-dataset gradient (47\% $\to$ n.s., 18\% $\to$ $+0.42$~pp, 14\% $\to$ $+1.36$~pp) is consistent with an inverse relationship ($n{=}3$ datasets), with stronger grounding from per-entity-type analysis ($\rho{=}{-}0.881$, $p{=}0.004$, $n{=}8$; Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
Temperature manipulation provides the cleanest test ($T{=}1.2$: degeneracy 12.5\%, $\rho{=}0.225$; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}), altering output diversity without changing model capacity.
LoRA rank${=}8$ (degeneracy 7.2\%, $\rho{=}0.24$) corroborates the pattern, though this ablation conflates diversity with capacity; both confirm that alignment is largely task-determined, and degeneracy reduction alone cannot unlock LP selection on datasets with weak alignment.

\paragraph{Practical guidelines.}
Practitioners should first estimate instance degeneracy on a labeled subset (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}): in the high-degeneracy regime (${>}$30\%), prefer greedy decoding; structural signals still support quality estimation ($\rho{=}0.43$--$0.47$).
In the low-degeneracy regime (${<}$15\%) with adequate alignment ($\rho \gtrsim 0.3$), LP selection is effective and scales with $N$ ($+1.36$~pp on Few-NERD; $+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16).
Temperature provides a controllable lever for degeneracy (40.3\% at $T{=}0.5$ to 12.5\% at $T{=}1.2$; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}) but cannot address alignment; training convergence offers a second lever (Few-NERD degeneracy rises from 11\% to 31\% between 3 and 5 epochs, halving LP gains; on SciERC, 3-epoch training yields 6.4\% degeneracy with FK $\rho{=}0.53$, SJ $\rho{=}0.52$, vs.\ 17.8\% and FK $0.27$, SJ $0.36$ at 5 epochs; Table~\ref{tab:epoch_confound}).
Standard calibration methods preserve within-instance argmax and cannot change selection; even multi-feature variants yield no improvement ($p{=}0.31$--$0.83$; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration_baseline}), confirming the bottleneck is alignment rather than miscalibration.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal; even supervised combination of the five signals studied does not close the oracle gap (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}).
Effective selection requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}; $N{=}8$ captures most QE benefit (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
Structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).

Our evaluation covers four NER datasets; an exploratory RE extension on SciERC is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension} but generalization to other RE benchmarks remains unvalidated.
We cover 4B\textendash 8B scale; whether the gap holds for 70B+ models or closed-source APIs is untested. Larger models may produce more diverse samples.
We do not train a verifier, leaving unknown how much oracle headroom a supervised approach could recover.

We evaluate at $N{=}8$ (primary) and $N{=}16$; behavior at larger sample sizes is unknown (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
The free-form ablation covers SciERC NER and CoNLL NER with one model; RE free-form results are in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint used empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks; a three-part analysis rules out this confound (Appendix~\ref{app:thinking_token}).
LP compression worsens on easy datasets at lower temperature (CoNLL tied fractions reach 95.8\% at $T{=}0.7$); whether reduced temperature translates to selection gains remains untested.
We tested verbalized confidence \cite{tian2023calibration} as a second per-sample signal; it exhibits severe overconfidence (mean 8.58/10 on SciERC, 9.24/10 on CoNLL) and yields the weakest QE and selection among all signals (Appendix~\ref{app:verbalized_confidence}).
Ad-hoc LP${\times}$VC combinations yield at most $+0.2$~pp over greedy (not significant; \S\ref{sec:discussion}); whether \textit{learned} combinations could close the gap remains open.
The $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold used for tied/non-tied LP stratification is a post-hoc exploratory choice; while selection F1 is stable across $\varepsilon \in [0, 0.2]$ (Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}), the specific subset gains should be interpreted as characterizing the compression phenomenon rather than as a tuned selection strategy.
We tested one remedy for LP compression (entity-token-only LP, excluding format/schema tokens) which fails to improve selection despite increasing within-instance variance on SciERC ($4{\times}$); LP${\times}$VC combinations also fail to recover selection (\S\ref{sec:discussion}); calibration-based approaches remain unexplored.
Our selection experiments use 2 training seeds (stability $\sigma{\leq}0.026$); while within-seed statistical power is high ($n{=}32{,}565$ for Few-NERD), training seed stochasticity is not exhaustively quantified.
Few-NERD models are trained for 3 epochs (vs.\ 5 for other datasets) due to earlier convergence; a 5-epoch control experiment is provided in Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound} to verify that degeneracy differences are not training-induced.

\paragraph{Practical guidelines.}
Practitioners should first estimate instance degeneracy on a labeled subset (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}): in the high-degeneracy regime (${>}$30\%), prefer greedy decoding; structural signals still support quality estimation ($\rho{=}0.43$--$0.47$).
In the low-degeneracy regime (${<}$15\%) with adequate alignment ($\rho \gtrsim 0.3$), LP selection is effective and scales with $N$ ($+1.36$~pp on Few-NERD; $+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16).
Temperature provides a controllable lever for degeneracy (40.3\% at $T{=}0.5$ to 12.5\% at $T{=}1.2$; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}) but cannot address alignment; training convergence offers a second lever: on Few-NERD, degeneracy rises from 11\% to 31\% between 3 and 5 epochs, halving LP gains (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_confound}); a SciERC 3-point curve (3, 5, 10 epochs) shows both conditions degrading in tandem, with degeneracy rising from 6.4\% to 47.8\% while within-instance alignment collapses ($\rho$ 0.317 $\to$ 0.120), confirming that signals are most effective in the moderate training regime (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc}).
Standard calibration methods preserve within-instance argmax and cannot change selection; even multi-feature variants yield no improvement ($p{=}0.31$--$0.83$; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration_baseline}), confirming the bottleneck is alignment rather than miscalibration.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal; even supervised combination of the five signals studied does not close the oracle gap (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}).
Effective selection requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}; $N{=}8$ captures most QE benefit (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).

\section{Epoch Confound Analysis}\label{app:epoch_confound}

\paragraph{Training convergence modulates degeneracy.}
Table~\ref{tab:epoch_confound} compares the 3-epoch model (used throughout the main text) with a 5-epoch variant on Few-NERD (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$).
Extended training increases greedy F1 by $+2.95$~pp (0.748 $\to$ 0.777) but nearly triples instance degeneracy (11.1\% $\to$ 31.3\%), reducing the fraction of instances with non-degenerate outputs from 85.6\% to 68.7\%.
LP selection gains drop correspondingly ($+1.37$~pp $\to$ $+0.62$~pp), consistent with the degeneracy-gating mechanism identified in the main text (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Within-instance LP-quality alignment is relatively stable under this convergence shift (mean $\rho$: $0.524 \to 0.407$; median $\rho$: $0.667 \to 0.615$), consistent with alignment being determined primarily by task structure rather than training duration.

Evaluation loss increases after epoch 3 (0.032 $\to$ 0.041 at epoch 5), and the best checkpoint by validation loss occurs at step 32{,}000 (approximately epoch 3.9).
Standard early stopping practice thus naturally selects the low-degeneracy regime where LP selection is most effective.
This finding refines the narrative: degeneracy is not a fixed property of datasets but is modulated by the degree of training convergence. Over-trained models compress their output distributions, collapsing diversity even on datasets that support it under well-regularized training.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Training convergence confound on Few-NERD (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). ``Degen.'': constant-F1 instance degeneracy (gold-filtered). ``Valid'': fraction of instances with non-degenerate outputs. ``$\rho$ mean/med'': within-instance LP-quality correlation. The 3-epoch model corresponds to standard early stopping; the 5-epoch model is a controlled ablation.}
\label{tab:epoch_confound}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Metric & 3-epoch & 5-epoch \\
\midrule
Greedy F1 & 0.748 & 0.777 \\
Instance degen.\ (\%) & 11.1 & 31.3 \\
Valid instances & 3{,}723 / 4{,}351 (85.6\%) & 2{,}988 / 4{,}351 (68.7\%) \\
LP $\Delta$ (pp) & $+$1.37 & $+$0.62 \\
Within-inst.\ $\rho$ (mean) & 0.524 & 0.407 \\
Within-inst.\ $\rho$ (median) & 0.667 & 0.615 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{SciERC epoch curve.}
Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc} extends the analysis to SciERC with a 3-point curve (3, 5, 10 epochs; Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$).
Degeneracy increases monotonically (6.4\% $\to$ 17.8\% $\to$ 47.8\%), but critically, within-instance LP-quality correlation also degrades: median $\rho$ drops from 0.317 at 3 epochs to 0.120 at 10 epochs, indicating that overtraining erodes both necessary conditions simultaneously.
At 10 epochs, the model retains competitive greedy F1 (0.649 vs.\ 0.650 at 3 epochs) with 8.4~pp of oracle headroom, yet LP selection yields only $+0.75$~pp, consistent with weak within-instance alignment ($\rho{=}0.120$) rather than effective signal exploitation.
This pattern validates the two-condition framework (\S\ref{sec:discussion}): at 10 epochs, condition~1 is violated (47.8\% degenerate) and condition~2 is compromised ($\rho{=}0.120$).
The gradient confirms that consistency-based signals are most effective at moderate training convergence; extended training compresses output distributions, degrading both diversity and within-instance alignment.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{SciERC NER epoch curve (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Training duration modulates both instance degeneracy and within-instance LP-quality alignment. ``Degen.'': constant-F1 instance degeneracy (gold-filtered). ``$\rho$ med'': median within-instance LP-quality correlation.}
\label{tab:epoch_scierc}

Metric & 3-epoch & 5-epoch & 10-epoch \\
\midrule

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluate five confidence signals for quality estimation and sample selection in LLM-based NER across four benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient.
All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.42, AUROC up to 0.82), supporting selective prediction.
For selection, LP achieves $+1.36$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) when two conditions are jointly met: low instance degeneracy (${<}$15\%) and adequate LP-quality alignment ($\rho \gtrsim 0.3$); gains scale with sample budget ($+0.52$~pp, $N{=}8{\to}16$, $p{=}0.003$).
When either condition is violated, selection does not improve over greedy decoding despite 12\textendash 14~pp oracle headroom: at 17.8\% degeneracy with weak alignment ($\rho{\approx}0.24$; SciERC), $+0.42$~pp ($p{=}0.091$, below the MDE); at 47.4\% (CoNLL), LP does not improve.
Two mechanisms block selection: instance degeneracy (14\textendash 47\% of instances yield identical F1) eliminates headroom, and weak LP-quality alignment prevents exploiting the remainder.
Structural signals do not improve selection regardless of degeneracy, and supervised combination of the five signals studied does not close the oracle gap; within these signals, the bottleneck is in what they encode, not how they are combined.
Whether these patterns persist at 70B+ scales remains open.
Closing the gap for structural signals likely requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers}; LP provides a practical baseline when both conditions are met, with degeneracy controllable via temperature and training convergence.

\begin{abstract}
Self-consistency yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where no majority vote analog exists.
We evaluate five confidence signals (four instance-level, one per-sample log-probability [LP]) for quality estimation and sample selection on four NER benchmarks using 4B\textendash 8B models.
All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.42, AUROC up to 0.82), supporting selective prediction.
For selection, LP achieves significant gains under two jointly necessary conditions: low instance degeneracy and adequate LP-quality alignment ($\rho \gtrsim 0.3$), yielding $+1.36$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) with gains scaling with $N$ ($+0.52$~pp, $N{=}8{\to}16$, $p{=}0.003$).
When either condition is violated, selection does not improve over greedy decoding ($T{=}0$) despite ${\sim}$13~pp oracle headroom, a disparity we term the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
Two mechanisms block selection: \textit{instance degeneracy} (14\textendash 47\% of instances yield identical F1 across all samples) eliminates headroom; \textit{weak LP-quality alignment} prevents exploiting the remaining headroom.
A methodological observation underlies both: four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that cannot rank candidates by construction.
Degeneracy is controllable via temperature and training convergence; closing the gap for structural signals likely requires learned per-sample scoring.
\end{abstract}

1	\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
2	
3	Self-consistency (majority voting over multiple samples) yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning \citep{wang2023selfconsistency}, and test-time compute scaling has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
4	But named entity recognition (NER) poses a structurally different challenge: the output is a \textit{set} of entities, two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and there is no obvious majority to vote on.
5	
6	Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) with \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
7	Existing self-consistency methods \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc, taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence, an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
8	Unlike \citet{yao2026consistency}, who demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy, we investigate \textit{why} this correlation fails to yield selection improvements, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as the two blocking mechanisms.
9	Our experiments use fine-tuned models, the dominant deployment paradigm for production NER, and separate quality estimation from best-of-$N$ selection.
10	
11	A methodological premise structures our analysis: four of five signals (SJ, VC, FK, EM) are instance-level aggregates that by design assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates for a given input; only log-probability (LP) is natively per-sample.
12	All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.42, AUROC up to 0.82; Figure~\ref{fig:overview}), supporting selective prediction.
13	For selection, LP achieves $+1.36$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) when two conditions are jointly met: low instance degeneracy (13.8\%) and adequate alignment ($\rho{\approx}0.5$), with gains scaling with $N$ ($+0.52$~pp, $p{=}0.003$).
14	This success does not generalize: on the primary test bed, selection does not improve over greedy decoding ($T{=}0$) despite 12\textendash 14~pp oracle headroom, a disparity we term the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
15	Two mechanisms block selection: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy} (14\textendash 47\% of instances yield identical F1 across all $N$ samples, eliminating headroom); and (b)~\textit{weak LP-quality alignment} (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ too low to exploit the remaining headroom; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
16	
17	\begin{figure*}[t]
18	\centering
19	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
20	\caption{The correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals reliably predict instance-level quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL, 0.38 on the primary test bed, 0.42 on Few-NERD; AUROC up to 0.82). \textbf{Right}: quality estimation does not translate to selection; all methods approximately match greedy decoding ($T{=}0$) despite 13~pp oracle headroom (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).}
21	\label{fig:overview}
22	\end{figure*}
23	
24	We evaluate five signals from three families (structural, surface, and model-internal) on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc} as a primary medium-difficulty test bed, with Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (low-degeneracy contrast), CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (ceiling-effect control), and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (signal-collapse boundary), using two 8B models (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B) with a 4B ablation (Qwen3-4B).
25	We vary candidate pool size ($N{\in}\{2,\ldots,32\}$), signal sophistication, and model capacity within the 4B\textendash 8B range; behavior at 70B+ scales remains an open question.
26	An exploratory extension to relation extraction is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
27	Our contributions:
28	\begin{enumerate}
29	    \item \textbf{Quality estimation framework and a methodological observation.}
30	    Five signals from three families evaluated on four NER benchmarks, two model families, and a 4B ablation, achieving reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.42; AUROC up to 0.82).
31	    A key observation: four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that cannot rank candidates by construction; this per-sample vs.\ instance-level distinction separates signals that can, in principle, improve selection from those that cannot.
32	
33	    \item \textbf{Two mechanisms underlying the correlation-selection gap.}
34	    Instance degeneracy (14\textendash 47\% of instances yield identical F1) eliminates headroom for consensus-based selection; weak LP-quality alignment (within-instance $\rho{\approx}0.24$) prevents exploiting the remaining headroom.
35	    Diagnostic ablations (temperature, LoRA rank, entity-token LP, supervised combination) confirm the bottleneck lies in the signal space within the five signals studied.
36	
37	    \item \textbf{Conditions for LP selection and practical guidelines.}
38	    LP achieves $+1.36$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) and scales with $N$ ($+0.52$~pp, $p{=}0.003$) when both conditions are met: degeneracy ${<}$15\% and alignment $\rho \gtrsim 0.3$.
39	    Per-entity-type analysis provides statistical grounding ($\rho{=}{-}0.881$, $p{=}0.004$, $n{=}8$); temperature and training convergence offer controllable levers for degeneracy.
40	\end{enumerate}
41
